title: A Simple Way To Build Rapport With Difficult Students students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recommends a subtle, low-key strategy for connecting with difficult students who are guarded and skeptical after years of failed teacher tactics: a short, handwritten, genuine note left on or near their desk. He warns against coming on too strong with forced friendliness, since these students see through insincerity quickly. The note's content matters less than its genuineness — simple, brief statements of belief in the student, left privately without follow-up commentary. He advises against watching the student read it or making a big deal of it afterward, letting the moment remain private. Used sparingly, not as a daily gesture but occasionally when it feels right, these notes build organic trust and open a channel of rapport that direct interaction often cannot reach.
points: Difficult students are often guarded and skeptical of overly friendly, forward approaches from unfamiliar adults.
A short, handwritten, genuine note left privately on a student's desk can build rapport more effectively than direct interaction.
The note's sincerity matters more than its content; false praise or manipulation will backfire immediately.
Teachers should not watch students read the note or make a big deal of it afterward — the moment should remain private.
These notes should be used sparingly, once or twice early in the year and then only when it feels genuinely right.
quotes: One of the most effective ways to do this is with a simple note, written in your hand, folded over, and taped to the top or side of their desk.
What you say in your note is less important than its genuineness. For if you don’t truly believe what you say, your students will find you out.
You mustn’t mention the note to the student and it’s best not to watch them while they read it.
An oft-repeated phrase on this website is that there is no magic to your classroom management plan. And it’s true.
A simple note, though, just between the two of you, has a way of cutting through their negative views of school and of teachers.
